projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Thomas Wilson Reese was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Please state your full name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Thomas Wilson Reese.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Please state your date of birth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: [birthdate redacted].

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Please state your current address.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: [address redacted].

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Which war or wars did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: World War II and Korean War.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Which branch of the service did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: In the U.S. Navy.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: What was the highest rank that you achieved?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Chief electrician's mate, normally called as EMC.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Mr. Reese, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Where were you living at that time?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Lewiston, North Carolina, in Bertie County.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Why did you join the Navy?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: I had a good friend who was in school, and he was two grades ahead of me, and I asked him what he was going to do when he got out. He says, "I'm going to join the Navy and be an electrician." That influenced me to join the Navy and to be an electrician.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Can you tell me about your boot camp training experience?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, I was trained in Norfolk, Virginia, close -- well, 100 miles from where I raised, and they started out with some things that I was not quite used to, such as sleeping in hammocks instead of on a bed. But we each had our own hammock, and we had the hammocks secured to each other to keep them from dumping us. But I got used to it after a little while, and I asked the chief who was my boss, company boss, if after a due time -- you were supposed to be restricted from going home -- I said, I live a hundred miles, I've got my uncle lives here in Norfolk, he's going down, can I go with him? He says, "All right." So I got to go spend the weekend with my parents during the boot training.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: And in what year was this?

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: The one that I had, the chief I was talking about, was named Baker. Yeah. And little short fellow. But very straight and very good, too. Everything was just so, so, was the way he was going. But he was -- he was good. He set good examples for us. But here I was, a rookie from the country and knowing nothing about the military, I was open for suggestions and ideas on how and what I should do. And I tried to do the best I could in that regard.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Did you find it difficult to get through boot camp?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Not really. I gained a little weight from eating regular. The meals, they ate at certain times, and so I gained a little weight. But not -- I didn't find it difficult. I was in pretty good shape and enjoyed it in a way. But then I had to go -- graduation, then we'll send you to the USS Whitney (AD-4), which was in Norfolk for a repair, overhaul, but its home port was San Diego.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Now, this was your first duty assignment after boot camp?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: That's correct, yeah. And I hadn't been on a ship before, so -- and as I mentioned, the waves sort of got me, rocking around, and got seasick a couple times. But, anyway, we got on the run, and I wanted to be, as I say, an electrician. We finally came through the Panama Canal and came on around here to San Diego, to our home port, and after a certain length of time, a number of years, why, they allowed me to get -- to do -- to go into electrical work, and where I'd learn to wind electrical motors and transformers and armatures and so forth, is really what I wanted to do. So . . . And I stayed in that, and it's paid off.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Did you go to electrician's school, or was this on-the-job training?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Most of it was on-the-job training, but in later years I did get to go. After I was chief, even, I went to electrical school. I was with the training command in San Diego here. And the captain in charge said, "Have you ever had any schools?" And I said no. He said, "What school would you like to go to?" So I went to advanced electrical school in Chicago.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: How long were you aboard the USS Whitney? THOMAS REESE: Well, I went aboard in June of '34 and left it in '41. So about seven years.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: What was your next duty assignment after the USS Whitney?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: The USS Hornet (CV-8) was being built in Newport News, and I -- on the Whitney, they asked for personnel for -- to go on as a crew, and I volunteered along with eight other fellows to go aboard the Hornet, which was being built in Norfolk. And it was commissioned on the 20th of October of 1941.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: What was your job assignment aboard the USS Hornet?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, being an electrician, I was assigned to some electrical auxiliary equipment to start with on it, and such as the steering gear equipment at the auxiliary area and then also some of the fire rooms and engine room electrical motors and equipment, I had assignments to that.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: How long were you aboard the USS Hornet?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: They put it in commission on the 20th of October of '41 and it was sunk on October the 26th of '42. That's how long I was aboard.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Now, you were aboard the USS Hornet during the Doolittle Raid, weren't you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: You bet you.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Can you tell me about that experience?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, after we got -- we got them aboard and -- at Alameda on April the 2nd, we got his group aboard, and then we went on out till the 13th of April and met the Enterprise (CV-6), and with escorting ships, we had the escorting ships there, and that's when they were told that we -- what our mission was. And then from that point on, they said -- made us Task Force 16. And then we went on to start on our mission. And then as I mentioned earlier, when the -- about 650 miles out, they spotted us, and they told the air personnel to fill all cans on the Hornet that could get -- with gasoline and pump the air out of the tanks of the planes, because they were going to have to launch them long before they had -- the United States had made arrangements with General Chiang Kai-shek in China for Doolittle planes to land in -- bomb Japan and land in China when they got within about 400 miles, 450. But they -- as a result of that, they'd got to bomb eight places in Japan. Three of the Doolittle people were lost. They -- when they got out of the -- planes crashed and so forth. But eight of them were captured, and that's when these fellows who captured them said, "Let's execute them." But the emperor said, "No, execute three of them." They was -- supposedly those three dropped bombs on schoolyards. So the other five went to prison, solitary confinement, for 40 months. They were to stay in there, or did, four of them did. Lieutenant Meder of the five died doing that 40 months. But four of them lived through the war, and after 40 months they were released. And that's when Jake DeShazer, I told you was a minister in Salem, Oregon, today, he was one of those four.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Can you tell me about some of those battles that you were involved in?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Yeah. I can tell you now, this is in Guadalcanal, for example. The battle at Guadalcanal, that's the Hornet, but it was set -- it was -- August the 7th of '42 the battle of Guadalcanal started. On the 17th of August, the Hornet took some marine planes and pilots over. They were having a rough time, and there's a book now called A Ship to Remember, and on page 229, the marines says, "Marines will tell you that the Hornet saved Guadalcanal." So . . . Then on June -- the June prior to that, we were in the battle of Midway, and the battle -- we -- on my ship, we lost all of top Peter (ph) aid except one. Ensign Gay was the only one. And I've had the opportunity to meet with him, and I have his book also on his experiences.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: And this was while you were aboard the USS Hornet?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Hornet, uh-huh. Right. Yeah. And that was in June. The battle of Philippine -- I mean Midway was June 4 to June 7, and it ended June 7 with the battle. The Yorktown (CV-5) got sunk in the carrier. Now, it had been damaged in the Battle of the Coral Sea on May 8 of '42, when the Lex (CV-2) was sunk, and it had been damaged. It came back to Honolulu, and Admiral Nimitz was in charge. The yard workers told Admiral Nimitz it would take about two months to get the flight deck fixed. He said, "You have three days." So they put metal plates over the flight deck and so we could go into the Battle of Midway and have battle in there. And they did. And like I say, on the 7th it was sunk. And that's been on television, too. They had that deal. And I wanted to say, also, that there was a destroyer that was helping the Yorktown, it was Hammann. Hammann, and it got some depth charges knocked off of its ship and it -- as a result, they lost a lot of their men from this that was trying to help take the Yorktown. But -- take the men off or whatever they could do to help them. But it was gone.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Were you -- you were aboard when the ship was sunk?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: When -- we abandoned ship, then they finally -- it was -- got damaged so bad that we had to abandon ship.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Tell me about the experience that led to that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Yeah. Well, the -- I have the -- see, since we took Doolittle for the first attack on Japan on April the 18th of '42, our government -- the Japanese did not know where those Army planes came from, so they had -- when the ship was one year old, our captain gave a dinner for us, and he told us that the Japanese had found out that the Doolittle raiders came from our ship, the Hornet (CV-8), and they issued orders to the Japanese fleet to get us at all cost. And on the morning of the 26th of October of '42 at 9 o'clock they started hitting us, and when the day was over, we had four bombs, three torpedoes, and two planes that had hit us. And the captain had us abandon ship at about 5 o'clock in the afternoon. And as I -- before I abandoned ship, I was -- had come up from my battle station, which was the forward engine room, and -- the electrician for that. And as I turned around from the side and looked, the chief engineer had been blown up and was standing by a railing, but there were -- two men down the ladder going to the next deck were yelling for help. And I looked for the chief engineer to see, because officers always give orders. But I -- he was shook as a result of coming up. So I told the man hanging on the ladder that I would -- I was coming down and I'd pull him out. He was hanging on the ladder and had oil and water all over him. I said, "I'm going to hold you by the web belt. I'm not turning you loose of the rungs of this ladder, but when you feel me pull, you let go." And I pulled him up to the hangar deck level. Then I went to the next set of ladders going down where the man was hanging, and I did the same thing for him, pulled him up and got him up. And then as I started walking across the hangar deck, one of the water tenders from the fire rooms who knew I had been working with them says, "Reese, this man is yelling for help on the other side of the elevator pit." And I could hear him. He said, "We can't let him stay there." So I turned around to the lockers there where the boatswain's mates, the ship's boatswain's mates, keep their lines, and we got the lines and we tied them together and we kept throwing them over, because the water was going quite high where the torpedo had hit in this elevator pit. And so finally we got the lines over there and told him put it around him, and he did. Then he fought us. The two of us pulled him across, but we pulled him across and got him across there. And so as a result of that, then the ship was listing 18 degrees and oil was all over the hangar deck. We could not walk across the hangar deck. The mate below on the hangar deck tied lines on it, and we pulled ourselves across the top side of -- the portside so that we could go over the side when we got ready to abandon ship. And then later on, in the water, we got in the water, and they teach you with your life jackets to get on your back, get out of the water. So we did that as much as possible, and as I did that, I saw six out of the two bombers coming over, and I never saw the planes again, but I saw five bombs come. My little prayer was, Hit the ship and go on to the other side, don't come in the water where we were. And just -- I had what was official in the story, and that's just about what happened to him. But the men in the water were arguing about something, and there was a life raft, which is a big egg-shaped life raft, and I said, "Fellows, our lives are at stake. If that ship sinks, it's going to take us with it. Let's get on that raft and get out." And one of the men who was -- there's four or five of these fellows were electricians, one of them was named Blanco (ph). Blanco (ph) said, "I can't swim, Reese." I said, "You don't have to swim, we'll lift you up and put you in the raft." So we did. So I told the rest, two of the electricians, "You get on one side of the raft with the paddle, one get on the other side with me, and the other fellows hold to the lines and kicked us off and let's get out of there." And that's how we got out. And eventually we got out to where the Destroyer Mustin (DD-413) picked up 337 of us.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: How long were you in the water?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: I estimate about an hour. It wasn't very long. One of the electricians swam by as we were on the raft going out, his name was Jerry. I said, "Jerry, where are you going?" He said, "San Francisco, next stop." He was swimming, and here we were paddling, trying to get away from it. But, anyway, that's about what we were in there, about an hour in there. And they had other ships picking up other men, too, see.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: What happened next?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, I read some history, early history of World War I, that said that the life of a destroyer was 15 minutes, and here I was on the destroyer, and I was more frightened on that destroyer than I had been with all of this action on the Hornet, because the Hornet was so big, you could take care of yourself in water-tight compartments and all of that. So I ran from one end to the other of that destroyer to see where I thought might be the safest spot to be. I wound up in probably the worst spot. That was down in midship, down on the gratings of the engine room, in the fire -- yeah, in the engine room. But, anyway, the orders -- the ship got orders -- the ship got orders to fire 5-inch shells in to try to sink the ship that was still listing, still floating. And they put -- and this is official records -- 369 rounds of 5-inch shells in it, and that evening the Japanese came with two subs, two torpedoes, and that was the final sinking of it. Then I got orders from there to go to the Lexington that was being built in Boston.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Mr. Reese, tell me about your most memorable experience aboard the USS Hornet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, I think the most after the torpedo hit was to -- saving the two guys and then getting -- having to get off the ship to swim away after the torpedoes had done the damage and the bombs had done the damage to the ship. That was the most. I can still see myself out there swimming now, trying to get away from the ship. But it -- it was a wonderful ship, and it was -- but that was -- saving these two guys. And by the way, Lyle Styson (ph), who was the guy that was given a cross for risking his life to save this man that Lyle Styson (ph) and I pulled across from the other side of the midship elevator. Several have told me that I should have told that some other place, but I didn't. But it's -- I helped him, Lyle, to pull the guy across. But he's passed away. But I was shown the records. His wife showed the records to one of the fellows on the destroyer that lives up in Solana Beach that picked me up, and he showed me the letter that -- and the citation. And in the Admiral Nimitz Museum in Fredericksburg, Texas, is the story of this fellow.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: So your next duty assignment was aboard the USS Lexington?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: CV-16, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: And in what year was that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: February the 17th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: And your job assignment aboard the Lexington --

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: -- was?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: In the electrical group. We had 150 electricians on there, and I was in the electrical group, and -- one of them doing -- working at the auxiliaries that has motors at various areas. They had 400 ventilation motors. I was in the group that had to take care of those. And then eventually I was assigned -- I made the rank where I could be first class, and I was in charge of that group, had 20 men of those 150 were in my group. And then one day later on, well, a torpedo hit us on the -- December of '43 and knocked off one of the screws. And then the -- we got orders -- and the steering gear was part of my responsibility. We had 185-horsepower motors, main motors, in the steering gear. And it had water. As a result of this hit with the torpedo, there was about 3 or 4 foot -- about 3 foot of water in the hatch that would close down on top of the four men that were in the steering gear, and so I told one of my men, Trahan (ph) and I, "Let's go back there and get the submergible pumps," which are designed to work under water and pump that water out. And so we did. We went back there and we pumped the water out. In the meantime, they had -- the people who were in there had righted the rudder. It was -- it was trying to do this to dodge the torpedoes coming in. But they corrected it to set it, and then the captain used one of the screws -- there were three screws left -- one of the screws to direct the ship and the others for the speed. And -- and in a little while the captain sat down, "In so many hours we'll be out of the enemy area and we'll be headed for home." So Honolulu was where we were going to get repairs. And that was -- that was in '43. '44, we were hit in the island structure with a plane.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Now, this is after you had left Honolulu and had repairs done?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: And had repairs.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: You went back out again?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Right. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Okay. And what happened then?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Yeah. Went back out, and we were going through the different stations that we were having battles with pilots going in, attacks of the islands, various islands, and one of the Jap planes hit into the island structure, but we -- fortunately, they had repair ships in the general area that could help, and others, too, that helped, and so we didn't have to come back in to Honolulu to -- so we could continue on with the battle.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: So you'd get repairs at sea?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, uh-huh. Did repairs. That was in November of '44 that occurred.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: And what happened next?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, I -- the admiral -- I had -- in '44. So I was, like as I said, made in charge of some of the equipment in that thing, and the -- one of the fellows -- I mean, we had some radio antennas and -- controlled by 20-horsepower motors, and we got word that one of the motors had burnt up, and so I went up to the catwalk where the motor was, and the first class that had charge of the motors, they were not in my group, but he knew I'd had rewind experiences, and this motor had been burnt up. So he asked me if I thought I could rewind it. And I said, "Yeah, if you have parts down in the storage to come up, then I can do it." So while we were standing there, the captain of the ship was standing on the flight deck, and the chief engineer behind us, and we heard the captain say to the chief engineer, "This is Sunday. We're going into battle Wednesday, and I want that motor running." He had no idea if I could get it going. But, anyway, this fellow, Lloyd from Georgia, was in charge. He got his men and brought it down into the electrical shop. I showed them how to disassemble it and make sure that they didn't damage the internal parts of it and so forth. In the meantime, he had checked and gotten the parts from the -- from the storage, and I started rewinding it. And I rewound it, and at 4 o'clock on Tuesday afternoon we had it on the test bench testing. And my boss was a pin stripe warrant, and he said, "Reese," my division officer named Iverson, he says, "you're going to have to -- "I'm going to have to make you chief." I said, "You're my boss." So, anyway, I had to take the exam for chief petty officer, and it went on from that. And then later on, after that, the division officer said, "I don't want this to happen to us again. You pick two of these men and teach them to rewind motors." And lo and behold, I did, and it went on fine that way. And years later I was at a re -- well, anyway, we taught them to rewind the motors. And then the -- actually, the -- after the motor was rewound, we went on with the rest of the battles in the area, see. And it worked out very good too.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Tell me about some of the battle engagements that you witnessed while you were aboard the USS Lexington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, we had the Solomons, we had Iwo Jima, we had -- there was several of them that was involved. And, of course, like I say, the -- oh, there was a number of them there. And I was -- I was thinking of the -- this was in '45, when the Admiral Nimitz -- not Nimitz, Mitscher was our admiral in charge of the 16 group out there. He was a small fellow, and he had ordered -- after I made chief, I was put in the IC -- what they call the IC room in charge of gyros, MC systems, and all of that sorts. He had requested or ordered that the -- up in the admiral's cabin on the bridge that these instruments that were spotted all around be put close so that he didn't have to walk all around the place. He was a small fellow. And so I was standing there on the catwalk outside, and my men were the ones who I had doing this. I had made chief at this time. And Commander Marbet, who was the chief engineer, and I were standing there and observing what they were doing and how they were doing it. And I asked Commander Marbet, who was a reserve and had been to Japan many times, if he thought the Japanese would ever give up. He said, "Never. They will fight until the last man." And so that was on the -- the 6th of August, is when we dropped the first atomic bomb, and on the 9th the second atomic bomb, and on the 15th of August they surrendered. And so we didn't know anything about the atomic bomb. But he said -- he says, "I've been there many times. I've ridden in their rickshaws, and they are not going to surrender." But, of course, after the atomic bombs did so much damage to them, and they did go ahead and surrender. So the Lexington was the first carrier to enter Tokyo Bay after they signed on the 2nd of September -- of December of '45.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: So what year did you return to the States?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, we returned to the States -- let's see. It was in the latter part of '45. And went into -- then they were going to put the ship out of commission later on, so I went up to Bremerton for that. And I was -- we were assigned to put -- put it out of commission. And so they -- after we got it out of commission, six chiefs and six officers and 60 men remained aboard to make sure everything is in. They put in the systems, see, for -- flooding systems to be prepared and taken care of and so forth. So I was one of the last to stay aboard. And one of my men in the IC group, they had installed -- the ship had installed the flooding mechanism systems that -- and they had the units spotted throughout the ship, and so he -- and we had what they call sound power phones, where it generated the sound power. And he suggested that we take the sound power leads down into the bilges area, and if water is coming in, we'd have an annunciator up that we took from the officers' quarters to put up on the quarter deck for the officers on the deck to have, and there were six places that they put these flooding systems. And so if one of those flooded, it would indicate and he'd know which one to send down. And they put this on the other ships up there, and as far as I know, I think they still have it today. But what they did, after they took the crew off the ship, they put a light on -- where the guards, the protectors up in the Bremerton area could -- if a flood -- you know, it would flash if something went wrong so they could go back on it. But they used his system. It was a very good idea. Later on and then this chief engineer who had been to Japan, Marbet, and I, he and I got along very well together, and two of my men, this fellow that suggested these systems, had gone up for chief. And another fellow is in charge of all the lighting in the area had gone up for chief. And I knew they did a good job on their test that they had taken, so I said to Commander Marbet, "We should make these fellows chief." He said, "They're cutting back in ranks now because the war's over, we ended the war." I said, "Do we punish those two fellows? They took the test with the idea of going up." A month later, I walked back, they were both sitting in the chief's quarters with chief's hats. They went through. And they both went out of the Navy, but they had taken -- they got their chiefs anyway. They passed the exam, so why shouldn't they?

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: What was your next duty assignment after the Lexington?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, let's see. The Lex. I got -- '45. I went to -- '47 I went to the naval station here in San Diego, and at that time, because of the war, they had taken the officers off of the ships, you know, and a lot of reserves left and went home. So they had chief petty officers as the supervisors and superintendents and assistant superintendents of the shops. So I was assistant superintendent of the electrical shop for the naval station 1947 to '49, in that area. And we had civilian personnel who would go aboard the ships and bring their equipment in, but our men -- and they would work on it in there. And we had gyro, whatever, the electrical motors, whatever they had to bring in from the ship to take care of. So I did that. Let's see. What, it's '50 then. Yeah. So I asked for Japan, to go to Japan. That's '49. I had asked to go have some duty over there.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: So you asked for a transfer?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: I asked for a transfer, yeah.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: And so later on I got it, and like I say, June of '50 is when the Korean War started. And I had -- they had approved of me, my duty going to Japan, because they have -- of what they call fleet sonar school here in San Diego, and they had a training command group in Japan and then Honolulu. And so I was on my way out to be the electrician for this command in Yokosuka, Japan. And the Korean War started, so General MacArthur stopped, rightfully, all dependent travels. And I was -- had planned to bring my wife and son out, but I couldn't do that because they stopped. And the people who were in Japan, the families who were in Japan, were -- as soon as they finished their time, they would come out. So we had to go. And so doing -- for 15 months I was on duty in Yokosuka, and I was the electrician for the group. The -- Russia had turned back seven patrol frigates that we had lent them during World War II, and they were in Yokosuka, and the chief engineer told me as soon as I got my bags unpacked, come back and -- come up to see him, and he wanted to give me the story on what they had to do with these things, because they were going to sell or give them to Brazil or the southern countries, areas down there, and we had to train them for that, personnel. So I went aboard these, one of them, and looked at the gyro, looked at the sound power systems, and looked at the MC system, and all the tags on them were in Russian. Everything I went, they were in Russian. So I turned one over, gyro, English. Gyro. And I went around and turned them all over. So I went and trained all, turned them all over. So they -- Brazil, for example, was one of the countries, and they'd have an officer and a man who was equivalent, could speak English, and they'd bring maybe 25 people or so, electricians, aboard. So I would -- after I familiarized myself with the electrical systems for the ship, I would yap to them what it was, and they would yap to their people, and after about two -- we would go out with them for about two weeks of training and see if they could handle it, and if they did, we'd let them go. So one place that -- Bangkok. One of the officers from Bangkok was a very, very -- all of them were very good, but for some reason or another, I took a liking to him. He could speak English pretty good. But he said, "If you ever come to Bangkok, look me up." He said. But, anyway, we did work that on and got all of those, and that was in the '50s. Then in -- after the -- '50 in Japan to '51 in -- September of '51, then I got -- got permission to be transferred to Honolulu in the same command, same group, but in Honolulu I could bring my wife and child out, see. Son out. So a man came just when I was -- a chief electrician's mate came from the fleet. He wanted to stay in Japan. So they let me go on. Let him take my place in Japan, and I went on and joined the group in Honolulu. And then after that group, I got through with that group, the headquarters out here at, like I say, for the sonar school, I got orders to go to that command. And then after that command, that's when the captain asked me if I'd had any electrical -- any schools, and I told him I'd been to schools -- I had not. And I went to the school. And in -- one of the things in the schools, every week you had a test, a multiple choice test and stuff, and then you had to do work. So one of the jobs one of the weeks was to wind electric motors. So we all went through with the process of winding our motors. And, of course, with my background, it wasn't much of a problem. So the instructor said when I got ready to leave, "I want your permission to use your sample for the future classes." I said, "I'd be honored." So that's it. So I went on. That was '54-'55. And I got duty down in six -- got duty in Pensacola, Florida. When I arrived in Pensacola, Florida, and they were making assignments on -- for me, they offered me, since I was a general service electrician's mate, and that was an aviation command, either go on shore patrol duty or be chief for the I and E, information and education office. They had just lost their chief in there. And I accepted the information and education office chief. And as a result of that, I reviewed the books, courses, and so forth that they had in there, and a lot of them were sort of obsolete, they were not current to the present situation. So I ordered to have trucks to come alongside. We were in the third floor of the building, and I just had our men, a half dozen of men in the group, to take all those old, useless books out, and we replaced them with new books in there. And then I had letters typed to send to 300 universities and colleges for their literature, because a lot of our officers and men wanted to take correspondence courses, and as a result, many, many came to our office to do that. And after we got this sort of set up, I went to the local schools, colleges, and high schools, wherever they would -- I could get information where if some of our -- we had 1200 people, roughly, in the command, where they could go over and take courses if they needed to. And I worked on that. So it worked out real good for that. And then one day later on -- we were the group, sort of a leader group, I guess, of the instructor training, and so we -- anyway, the officer in charge of all of the training for that command area called a meeting, and we had a meeting. And so -- and my boss was a lady, lady, it was Ms. Johnson. And, anyway, we were sitting there at the table, and we were going through various instructions and so forth. And the officer in charge, commander in charge, he said, "Well, I'm sorry, we can't do that because we don't have authority," so and so. And I said, "Commander, it just so happens that specification number so-and-so and paragraph so-and-so says so-and-so." He says, "Thank you, Chief." So he instructed to get -- the man to keep records. And after the meeting was over, he said, "Chief, I want to see you." So we walked on back, and Ms. Johnson was standing there with me, and he said, "Chief, I want to tell you," she said -- so-and-so, he said -- she said, "He is my chief." He said, "I just wanted to ask him a question. I didn't want him transferred to my command." So, anyway, we went on back from that. And she, Ms. Johnson, got relieved by Ms. Sacora (ph), and so Ms. Sacora (ph) was a very efficient -- both of them were very efficient ladies. They -- because they'd sit like you are there and I'm here, and we'd had a desk, books right here where we could communicate with each other. But, anyway, she said -- I had asked for certain commands and certain things to go when I was getting transferred, and so she says, "I'd like to write up a specification, you call it, give you a write-up on your experiences and so forth." And so she wrote a lot of information on how much I had done for the command and everything and background. And she had checked on and she had checked on, so forth. And she said, "It's chiefs like Chief Reese that has kept our Navy going," and so forth. And I started to bring you one of those copies, but I didn't. But, anyway, it was very good. And she went on -- I don't know whether you want this or not. She -- my wife came up and met her and her son -- our son. She says, "When I get married, I want a son like yours." But, anyway, I assume they're doing okay as far as that. And that was -- let's see. I retired, see, in November. And we had responsibility in that office, now, for administering the exams for -- the Bureau would send out exams and the officers would send out exams. We had to make sure that they were properly administered, see, through -- for the people that were taking the tests. And one fellow we had down there wanted to write a book on qualifications for the third-, second-, and first-class personnel, and since I was in the education office, he asked me if I would give him -- you know, give him some information to help him with the book, he was going to sell the book. He did. So, anyway. But, anyway, that -- on November, I believe it was November the 18th of '58 I retired, and then from that I went right on to college. When I got out of that, the Convair -- as I told you, I went to Remington Rand UNIVAC job, and then -- be interviewed, to be interviewed, and then when I was walking down the passageway, the guy said, You got -- where are you -- "What are you doing? You looking for a job?" I said yeah. And so then I went over and got interviewed at General Dynamics Convair Division and started working and retired from them in '77. In the meantime, San Diego had a city -- had what they called a Senior Citizens President's Council, and where the presidents of senior citizen clubs all in the county once a month would meet with this group, and this group would have people in the state all over, wherever they came from, to -- they wanted to get to the seniors, see. So they would come to this 15-member committee and give them the five- or ten-minute pitch. And if the presidents of the senior clubs who they met with, this committee, thought you had something that was real good, they'd invite this man or this lady to come to their club and tell their senior members about it. And so when I was in charge of my -- I was the president of my senior club out where I lived, and I went to it, and I wound up on this 15-member committee, Senior Citizens President Council for the city, and I served on it seven years. The last two years I was president of it, and during that time I had one fellow from New York come out to sell something to the senior citizens of the group. But it worked. And then while I was in that group, the last year or so, one of the fellows -- this state has what they call a Senior Legislature, California Senior Legislature. They have the same number of senators that the state has, the same number of assemblymen that the state has, but Senator Mello, Henry J. Mello, in 1981, told the -- our legislative personnel, "We must get some system set up whereby we can get our information direct to the seniors, not piecemeal." And as a result, the Senior Legislature came into California. Florida had had it before that time, and some others. 28 states have it now. But, anyway, we had it. So in -- my last year or so in the senior job there, one of our men -- San Diego County has two senior senators in this group, and at that time they had five -- an assembly person who represented one of the five supers of the districts, there were five, and we do have five. So the man who had the north -- the Senator who had the north part, Highway 80 is the dividing line, one Senator south, one north, and I live north, so this man was sick, so they asked me to run for the job, and I ran for the job and got it. A retired lady professor and two men and I ran. Went to 18 senior clubs to give our presentations, and I was -- the two men after -- somewhere along the line dropped out, but the lady and I, the professor and I, continued on. And I won the election. At that time, you had to have a two-year election. And so then I ran -- when the two years was up, I ran for that election again and was elected, and then two years was up, I ran for that, and so for six years I served as Senior Citizen -- Senator for the north part of San Diego County. And after that my wife says, "Don't you think that's enough?" So I called -- I called this lady professor, her name, I know it was Lee Smith, very nice, and told her I wasn't going to run anymore, would she be willing to run. And she did. And she got my job as a Senior Senator for the San Diego County. I don't know how long she stayed in. She lives up in the north part of -- Oceanside, I think it is. But that's it.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: So tell me, Mr. Reese, were you awarded any medals or commendations?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: I was awarded 12 medals. And then the citation that I think I -- I got -- the citation I got from the -- when I was with the education -- I and E office in Pensacola, Florida. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Do you belong to any veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Yes, I do. VFW and -- what is the one out in -- several of them, as far as that goes. I belong to one out in El Cajon and -- well, just I've got two or three of them I'm involved in that deal.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Can you tell me about some of the activities that you participate in with these organizations?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: I have -- I've written letters. I haven't really participated in, but I have written some letters. But not really -- I've written to different organizations, you know, and I tell them about some of the senior issues that I've been involved in, stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Mr. Reese, is there anything you would like to add that we have not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Well, I can't think -- I think you pretty well covered it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Carl Cox
sp.p: Mr. Reese, I would like to thank you for participating in the Veterans History Project, and I would like to thank you for your dedicated service to our country.

sp.speaker: Thomas Wilson Reese
sp.p: Thank you. Thank you very much. And I appreciate it. Yeah.
